description: LUNORIZON helps find lunar landing sites and dates with enough sunlight, battery power, and Earth contact. At the Moon’s south pole, terrain blocks the low Sun, and a landing delay can turn a workable plan into a power failure. We use NASA terrain and JPL ephemerides to compare options and find alternatives. We welcome teammates interested in lunar science, scientific computing, data visualization, and web development.
summary:
LUNORIZON is an interactive lunar landing planner that connects NASA terrain, sunlight, power and Earth communication in one decision workflow. Users choose a landing site, date and hardware configuration, inspect the mission hour by hour, and find alternatives when a delay breaks the plan.

Our demonstration makes the problem concrete: a seven-day delay at Haworth reduces continuous sunlight from a full 150-hour stay to just 8.9 hours, with power failing around hour 16. LUNORIZON finds six alternative sites for the delayed date—or the next passing date at Haworth.

The application combines 360° skylines, 3D terrain, site/date search, landing-footprint analysis, rover simulation and coupled engineering models. Shareable links and mission briefs preserve the reasoning behind each decision. LUNORIZON gives mission planners, educators and the public a clear path from NASA data to an actionable lunar landing plan.
details:
Try it: Open the website, select “Recover a delayed landing,” then choose “Use this site” to explore the replacement plan.
https://github.com/cs113062273-bot/NASA-Space-Apps-Challenge-2026

A landing date changes the mission

At the Moon’s south pole, nearby ridges control sunlight, solar power and communication with Earth. Changing the landing date or touchdown position changes these conditions throughout the stay.

LUNORIZON brings them together in an interactive desktop application. Users select a location, landing time, duration and equipment, then examine sunlight, battery charge, Earth visibility and data return. They can identify what breaks a plan, compare alternatives and apply a replacement directly.

1. Turn a landing delay into a concrete recovery decision

The central workflow compares the original plan, the delayed landing, another site on the delayed date and a later landing at the original site.

In our featured scenario, Haworth supports a 150-hour stay beginning on 11 January 2027. Landing seven days later leaves just 8.9 hours of continuous sunlight, with power running short around T+16 hours. LUNORIZON finds six passing alternatives among the compared Artemis III representative points. Keeping Haworth moves the next passing daily start to 26 May—128 days later.

Users can prioritize Earth visibility, gentler terrain, delay tolerance or lower battery capacity. When extra storage can resolve a power failure, the application calculates the required change and rechecks the plan.

2. See the terrain that controls the result

A 360° skyline places the Sun’s and Earth’s paths against surrounding terrain. Users can play the mission or drag the timeline to inspect critical moments.

A first-person 3D view shows terrain and celestial positions, apparent sizes and phases. Polar and whole-Moon maps provide sunlight, Earth visibility and terrain layers. Every view follows the same mission settings.

3. Calculate sunlight from NASA terrain and JPL ephemerides

LUNORIZON combines NASA LRO LOLA elevation products, LROC stereo terrain and NASA/JPL DE440 ephemerides processed through NAIF SPICE.

Curated skylines trace 720 directions across terrain extending to 300 kilometres, including lunar curvature. Illumination resolves the visible solar disk, terrain obstruction and eclipses caused by Earth. Site geometry includes parallax, light-time and aberration corrections.

Hourly ephemerides cover 2023–2031. Users can explore 30 curated locations—including nine Artemis III candidate-region points, polar ridges, Apollo sites and modern landers—or create a point from coordinates or the map.

4. Search systematically for a working site and date

The search evaluates selected candidates across up to 365 calendar days, applying mission requirements, hardware settings, minimum data return and maximum powered communication silence.

Users can inspect passing combinations or explore the Pareto frontier across landing date, slope, battery requirement, silence and returned data. Nominal and raised-skyline evaluations reveal sensitivity to terrain obstruction.

An annual heatmap exposes landing opportunities, while combined availability shows how maintaining several candidate sites expands the available dates.

5. Connect solar generation, storage, heating and radio demand

The power model tracks generation, consumption and battery charge, supporting vertical Sun-tracking, fixed and horizontal panels.

Storage settings include initial charge, depth of discharge, transfer efficiencies, power limits, heating and array derating. Results identify the first power shortfall, unserved energy and required battery capacity.

Radio and heater demand share the same electrical supply. An optional equipment-temperature model combines solar absorption, radiation, conduction, internal dissipation and controlled heating. Published Diviner data adds annual subsurface-mean and surface-maximum temperature context at supported locations.

6. Follow communication from antenna geometry to returned data

Direct communication checks lunar terrain clearance and Earth receiving elevation for three named DSN reference antennas.

S- and X-band link budgets include transmitter power, antenna gain, distance, receiver noise, lunar radio emission and modem limits. Users can select ground complexes, define daily allocations or import UTC contact passes.

Finite buffers track data generated, delivered, retained and lost. Relay planning adds separate lander-to-relay and relay-to-Earth contacts, independent buffers and Earth-arrival accounting. Bundled reference-orbit cases connect sampled geometry with editable RF requirements and service rates.

7. Evaluate where a lander fits

Native 5 m LOLA products support footprint analysis using slope, height, RMS uncertainty and return counts.

The application identifies connected terrain areas, the largest fitting circular footprint and available space at the exact mission point. Enabling the footprint requirement carries it into comparisons, date searches and delay recovery.

A separate ±500 m touchdown analysis reveals how landing offsets change sunlight, Earth visibility and slope conditions.

8. Bring local terrain into the calculation

Users can import lunar GeoTIFF elevation and quality layers while preserving source identity, coordinate registration and uncertainty fields.

Creating a mixed-terrain mission point retraces the skyline from the local observer height and recomputes sunlight, antenna visibility, power, communication and enabled thermal checks. Seven GeoTIFF export layers carry source and derived results into GIS workflows.

9. Drive a route through time

The terrain planner checks slope, grade, uncertainty sensitivity and clearance across the complete route width.

The moving simulation carries battery charge, temperature and payload queues through waiting, driving and a destination hold. Sunlight and contact are recomputed along the route; power, temperature or enabled mobility failures stop motion at the calculated position.

An optional wheel–soil model calculates traction, slip, sinkage, torque, wheel speed and drive power. Departure search finds the first passing sampled wait, evaluating nominal, raised-skyline and refined simulations together.

10. Make every decision inspectable and shareable

Mission settings persist across Plan, Delays, Compare, Engineering and Evidence pages. Share links restore the selected page and analysis inputs.

Mission briefs preserve the original plan, failure causes, alternatives, decision, sources and assumptions. CSV, JSON and GeoTIFF exports expose the calculations, with hashes identifying source data and results.

Validation includes 40 Sun/Earth comparisons with JPL Horizons, a maximum elevation difference of 0.00003°, a 300-point illumination comparison with NASA Goddard’s map showing a 2.46-percentage-point RMS difference, and Blue Ghost eclipse contacts matching reported times within four minutes. Automated suites contain 226 frontend tests and 33 Python tests.

Built for direct exploration

LUNORIZON uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js and Web Workers, supported by a Python pipeline with NumPy, SciPy, SpiceyPy, Rasterio and Shapely. It runs entirely in the browser with bundled scientific assets, without an account, API key or backend.

Its creative contribution is a complete decision workflow: explain the failure, find alternatives, apply a decision and carry the evidence forward. Mission planners can explore engineering trade-offs, educators can teach lunar geometry through interaction, and the public can discover how terrain and timing shape a mission.

AI assistance: Claude and OpenAI Codex assisted with application development, scientific data-processing pipelines, testing, debugging, documentation and presentation text. Numerical results are calculated from the cited NASA datasets and explicit engineering inputs.
